segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: OK, before you can understand how Bob's sister became the talk of the third grade and the big day that led to that people still remember, I need to explain first that Bob's sister is a drawing. segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: I went over to him and said put the picture away. I probably did that two or three times. And then the fourth time I went over, and I just took the picture and said, pay attention. It's math class.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: And I put it on my desk. He came up right before recess and was like, can I have my picture back? And I was like, what is this picture of anyways? And he said, it's Bob's sister. segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: I was like, don't worry. She's not going anywhere. She'll be right here. Anytime you want to see her, she'll be behind me.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Because the kids were into the picture of Bob's sister?

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: Yeah. And I didn't really quite understand why. I never investigated why this picture was such a big deal. But yeah, they would talk about it. They would go up and look at it. And, yeah, it was a thing.

segments.text: I really don't know what it is. It's a thing. I don't know what it-- it's lots of different things. You could think of it as a minion that looks weird. You could think of it as Fly Guy with no legs. You could think of it as Pac-Man ghost with big eyes.

segments.text: That's really funny.

segments.speaker: Antonio

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So Bobsister, gender unspecified, lived on the bookshelf near the photo of a wolf, until one week when Mr. Ablao went on vacation, and the kids had a substitute. segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: There's kind of all this speculation about what happened to Bobsister. Was she stolen? Was she murdered? Did she die? And so I go and I look a little bit. I looked under the desk. I looked behind the bookshelf and--

segments.text: [LAUGHS]

segments.text: There are all kinds of theories about what happened to Bobsister. Antonio and Dylan said it was really fun to talk about various abductors, including animals from an alternate universe. But Dylan says the prime suspect for his classmates-- that other picture on the bookshelf.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: I'm kind of vaguely annoyed because there's a lot going on in the school day, and I don't have much time to think about a picture of Bobsister. But they're kind of pestering me about it.

segments.text: And then one other student--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Dylan, actually.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: --pipes in and says, can we have a funeral for Bobsister? And I'm like, what are you talking about? And they're like, well, she died. Something happened.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: And I'm like, a funeral for Bobsister, a picture? And I say yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Probably just to get them to stop talking about Bobsister, but also, this is the kind of teacher he is. He says, sometimes, it's smart to take some detours, follow things where they lead.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: And they're like, when? I'm like, I don't know when. I don't know when this funeral's going to happen. And they're like, when? When's it going to happen? When's it going to happen? We are going to have a funeral for Bobsister. And so then, finally, I'm like, after recess on Friday.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That was Monday. The rest of the week goes pretty normally. Mr. Ablao sort of hoped that they would forget about the funeral by the end of the week, but no way. They're murmuring about it, preparing for it, which he has no part of.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The eight-year-olds are the ones organizing this and thinking it through. Finally, Friday arrives, the big day, the day of the funeral, kids come back into the room from recess.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: They're pretty giddy and pretty excited. So finally, I'm like, OK, game on, let's go. Funeral. I have no idea what is about to transpire. All of a sudden, boom, the tables kind of move out of the way.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: The leader of the funeral comes up with the stool. Two other students bring two tables and grab the flowers. Apparently, a bunch of girls had been making posters. They write Bobsister's Funeral on the board.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Dylan's the leader of the funeral, and he prepared a eulogy. So did his friend, Theo. Dylan gets in front of the class holding a microphone Mr. Ablao keeps in the room.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: The rest of the class is totally on the edge of their seats, just waiting for this kid to start the funeral, like, paying more attention to him than they had ever paid to me. They're just like, ready for it. He starts out kind of ad-libbing about welcoming everyone, thanking everyone for coming to celebrate the life of Bobsister.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Now, how did you know what to say in a eulogy?

segments.speaker: Dylan
segments.text: We didn't. We just said like some things that sounded about right. Like, something that you might say at a funeral that might make someone cry.

segments.text: Yeah. Take it out?

segments.text: Could you read it?

segments.text: OK, one sec. And then it sort of-- mine also says sort of back and forth she and he, so. Because I didn't really know. "Bobsister was a great person. People thought that Bob was just a drawing on a piece of paper, but I knew he was anything but that. But she is still in here. She made me think I could do things in school. If she was here today, she would say, keep on trying."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's really nice. It sounds like you were trying to be sort of inspiring.

segments.speaker: Dylan
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Dylan

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Whoa.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The other eulogy that Theo wrote was also really good. "I just want to say something about the special person here, Bobsister, how she was such a good friend to all the potatoes, and especially Mr. Potato Head." Potatoes were another fascination of Mr. Ablao's class that year. "What an honor it was to have her with us. God bless her." And then, from the back of the room, Mr. Ablao hears a boy crying.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: I would say almost wailing, but it was like a real cry. And at first, I'm thinking, oh my god, now they're just turning this into a joke. And then, I realized that he's actually seriously crying. Like, this is not a joke cry.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: And I walked back there. And everyone kind of turns back. Everyone's looking at both of us. And so I asked him. I'm like, what's wrong? What's going on? Why are you crying?

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: And he's like, it's because Bobsister died. And I was like, it's not about anything else, maybe? And he's like, no, it's Bobsister's died, and it's just so sad.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Mr. Ablao thinks maybe it was really about his dog. The dog that boy had grown up with had died just two weeks before. His mom had sent an email to let him know. But Mr. Ablao's really not sure. At eight, you're plenty old enough to catch a glimpse of what death means.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: And then I look up, and then the whole kind of feel of the classroom has changed. It's gone from kind of giddy excitement, this is a fun thing, to half the class is nervously laughing, and the other half looks like they're on the verge of tears. Like, there's about three girls that are kind of really sad.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: And I was like, oh no, what have I created? This was reaching an emotional level that I actually had never experienced before, and I've been teaching for about 15 years. And I had never felt kind of this-- not that it was getting out of control, but it was leading to something that I didn't know how it was going to end, honestly. Like, I don't know what's going to happen next. If three other kids start crying, I don't know how to handle the situation.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: I had never experienced kind of that in a classroom.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's so interesting. It's like they were playing around with, I don't know, like with a Ouija board and joking around, and suddenly, they accidentally summoned a demon into the room.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: Yeah. In a way. And for me, I was right there on the Ouija board with them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so this monster is in the room. You've unleashed this really kind of a primal force, like this grief, right?

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: Yeah. Grief, death. And I mean, one of the really neat things about third grade is it's-- I mean, there's a saying. "They stop learning to read and are reading to learn." So it's like it's an age where their world gets a lot bigger. They kind of are experiencing real things, and I think a funeral is one of those things.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: They probably all heard of a funeral. They read them in books. But most of them probably hadn't been to one and didn't know what that felt like.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And Mr. Ablao felt responsible to help them through this new experience, like he had lots of others that year. So he took control of the room back from the kids and addressed them all.

segments.speaker: Mr. Ablao
segments.text: I was like, well, funerals are kind of serious. Sometimes, when you go to a funeral, it's very sad because you're missing the person that's moved on. And sometimes, it reminds you of other people who have moved on. And it's important to remember those people, and it's important to be sad. And this is the end of the funeral.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Which worked. Everybody snapped out of it. The demon left the room. Next, was free time, which they all enjoy. And everything was fine.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But at the end of the school year, when the class stood in a circle and each kid names something that they remembered and liked from third grade, a couple of the kids said Bobsister's funeral. It was a moment for Mr. Ablao, too.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Sometimes, you're joking around and it's all light and fun and trying something you've never done before, and some bigger subterranean force gets unleashed. That's what our show is going to be about today-- those moments when you get a glimpse of all that feeling that's there down below, hidden from sight. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Act One, Music of the Night After Night After Night After Night After Night After Night After Night After Night-- [FADES AWAY]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So when you go to a big theater, you see all the people who are on stage-- they're brightly lit. They're visible to everybody. They are literally there to be seen.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But then, just below them down in front, there's the orchestra pit. And it seems straightforward enough what happens in there. Musicians play their instruments.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But other things go on in there, all kinds of interactions and feelings that usually we don't get much of a picture of. You know the old saying "hell is other people?" It actually comes from the theater, it comes from a play, No Exit.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That play was not written by somebody who sits in the orchestra pit. But Jay Caspian Kang has this story about how many musicians in theatrical orchestras might understand the sentiment. We first broadcast this story back in 2020. We are bringing it back today with an update. Here's Jay.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Nick Jemo moved to New York in 2006 to try to make it as a musician. He had just finished up college and had all these dreams of playing the trumpet for a living, but it was a struggle. There just aren't many jobs for trumpet players anymore. So he mostly waited by the phone for gigs.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Korean megachurch services, experimental plays, and the occasional substitute job with Mary Poppins on Broadway. And then a spot opened up at his favorite show.

segments.speaker: Nick Jemo
segments.text: This might be TMI, but I remember I was in my apartment. I was on the toilet. And [CHUCKLING] I got a phone call, and I didn't recognize the number. And I listened to the voicemail saying, "Hi, this is Kristen," and freaked out.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: This is one of the conductors for Phantom of the Opera. She offered him a job playing shows six days a week and twice on Thursdays and Saturdays.

segments.speaker: Nick Jemo
segments.text: I'm not sure I probably even let her finish her sentence. Yes, I'm very interested, very interested and available. It was life changing, really.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Did you feel like you'd won the lottery?

segments.speaker: Nick Jemo
segments.text: Oh, yes. Actually, I remember the next day, I had to go grocery shopping. And I remember buying coconut water. I don't know why. That was like my treat because I always wanted to buy coconut water, but it was always like too much of a-- I was like, you know what? I just don't need to spend. And I remember buying coconut water and feeling like such a bad ass.

segments.speaker: Nick Jemo
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Nick Jemo
segments.text: And I just felt like, I can buy anything here.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: It wasn't just a steady income Nick was excited about. Phantom of the Opera was a show Nick had loved since he was 11 years old. He had just started playing the trumpet and would lay on his living room floor listening to "The Music of the Night." You know it-- (SINGING) slowly, gently, night unfurls its splendor.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: That call changed his life. He had finally arrived, Phantom on Broadway. On his first day, Nick entered the Majestic Theater on 46th and 8th Avenue. He walked through a back alley past a giant tub of dry ice, down a flight of stairs into a locker room where he changed into all black.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: He then headed into the pit to play the music he had loved as a child. He had his own seat there now and a music stand. So he played the first show. Next day, he went back and played it again and then again.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: His brain started to adjust to playing the same show eight times a week. And then he started to notice, it wasn't just the music that repeated itself.

segments.speaker: Nick Jemo
segments.text: I'm seeing the same actors at the exact same time and the same musicians at the exact same time and seeing the same people in the bathroom at the exact same time.

segments.speaker: Nick Jemo
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Nick Jemo
segments.text: Every time one of the dancers comes through to put her wig on, she says to one of the other dancers, "Good job, Erica." Like every single day. It's very Groundhog Day.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: At first, this is funny, almost charming. Nick was 30 and the youngest person in the pit, not by a few years, but by a few decades. He'd never been in a situation like this where everyone seemed so locked into routine.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: His colleagues would sit down in their chairs at the exact same minute every day. There is a cellist who would say, "Marvelous," every time Nick asked him how he was doing. There was the first horn player who would pull out a stopwatch every single night to time how long the second horn player held a note in one of the songs. Some days it would be 17 seconds, other days 16.2.

segments.speaker: Nick Jemo
segments.text: You definitely start to notice, people are talking about each other and complaining about the same people are late every single week. If you bump into a stand by accident, you'll get like a "what the [MUTED] are you doing," kind of look? Like, [INHALES] take a deep breath. Like, [EXHALES]

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: What is it like being the youngest guy there, the young guy?

segments.speaker: Nick Jemo
segments.text: Basically, I'm not as jaded as the rest of them. If I say anything that's not like, [SIGHS] "it sucks to be here," they're like, "You haven't been here long enough. You're still new. You're still new." People kind of walk in there, like, [SIGHS], OK, I got to do this again. And some of it is just in their body language, the way they walk in the door. Like they're kind of trudging in. Or when someone says, "Do I have to do this tonight?"

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Phantom of the Opera opened on Broadway in January 1988. It was an instant hit.

segments.speaker: Barbara Walters
segments.text: Everyone who has seen this musical comes away enchanted.

segments.speaker: Newscaster
segments.text: The show is virtually guaranteed to run well into the next decade.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: It did. And then another decade, and another. The musicians in the pit signed contracts with the provision, which guaranteed their jobs until the show shut down. They expected two, maybe three years.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: But the show kept going, as three years turned into five years, which then turned into 32. That's over 13,000 performances. Phantom is now the longest-running show in the history of Broadway.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: There's almost a feeling, I think, of nausea, that you have to do it again, and you have to do it again.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: That's Melanie Feld, an oboist who's been in the pit for 28 years now.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: I don't know how to describe it-- a physical sensation that I get of, literally, that I'm jumping out of my skin. Like, it's a leg thing. I can't stand my skin. I'm going crazy. Oh, no, that thing is happening.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: I had first heard about the pit at Phantom through a friend, whose wife had recently subbed in the violin section. She described what she had seen as a horror show, like Waiting for Guffman, but 30 hard years down the line. I couldn't quite get it out of my head.

segments.speaker: Pete Reit
segments.text: So one of the first things people ask-- how can you possibly stay sane and play the same music every night?

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Pete Reit has been playing Phantom since opening night. He's the French horn player who times the notes on a stopwatch every night.

segments.speaker: Pete Reit
segments.text: Now, there is something in that, where you-- I would look at the music sometimes, and it would just literally look like shapes. I would just see, like, circles and lines and dots. And I would have no idea. I wouldn't even know what page I was on.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: It's like a dissociative feeling, almost. Like--

segments.speaker: Pete Reit
segments.text: It's sort of like hearing yourself speak, and you don't-- and you aren't sure it's English.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: (LAUGHING) OK, well, that is-- I don't think that's ever happened to me, Pete.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Pete Reit
segments.text: And then, the funny thing is, you see someone else do it, and you immediately know what's going on with them.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: What does their face look like?

segments.speaker: Pete Reit
segments.text: Oh, they're just like-- it's as if they don't even know where they are. They're, like, waking up in another room. It's like, what happened? Where am I? (LAUGHING) What day is it? What week is it?

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: When I started talking to the pit musicians a couple of years ago, I wanted to know how they found meaning in the mundane and inevitable repetitions of life. In lots of jobs, people do the same thing every day, but nothing quite like this. You're hearing the exact same lines from the stage, playing the exact same notes for the same songs.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Even the guy sitting next to you breathes in the exact same rhythm. Every day, the Phantom kisses Christine for the first time, and the same chandelier comes crashing down in the same spot on the stage.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: I assumed the orchestra members were like zen archers, who pull back the same bow, with the same motion, until they die. I talked to a trumpet player named Lowell Hershey. Lowell has been at the show since day one, and everyone says he's the sanest person in the pit.

segments.speaker: Lowell Hershey
segments.text: And it kind of drives you nuts for the first few weeks, and then after that, your mind deals with it and just flushes it out. So when you're not there, you don't think about it.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Do you know the words to the songs that you're playing?

segments.speaker: Lowell Hershey
segments.text: Uh, no. (CHUCKLING) Not entirely.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: "Where in the world--"

segments.speaker: Lowell Hershey
segments.text: "--think of me fondly." Whatever. I mean, I remember one time, after the show had been running for a while, somebody asked me to play a little bit of a tune from the show, and I couldn't even do it. I couldn't even think of one. (LAUGHING) I had submerged it so much.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: I feel like your brain has, basically, just rejected being cognizant that the music is going on.

segments.speaker: Lowell Hershey
segments.text: I think that's typical of people who do shows.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: What do you think the right type of personality is, that can handle this job?

segments.speaker: Lowell Hershey
segments.text: I'm descended from a long line of serfs and peons, you know, people who are used to laboring in the fields for hardly any money and are relatively happy with that.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: The Phantom players aren't exactly serfs. They're well-paid, they play a beloved show, and they get to play in small orchestras on the side. But these are highly trained musicians who went to the fanciest music schools in the world.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Andrew Lloyd Webber wanted the best of the best for Phantom, which means the pit will always sound good, though it also creates some creative and spiritual problems for the players, who have to get through the score night after night after night.

segments.speaker: Kurt Coble
segments.text: I'm a violin operator.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: [LAUGHS] Is that how you describe that?

segments.speaker: Kurt Coble
segments.text: That's how I describe it, yeah. You know, it's very technical. I have-- I have no emotional connection with it.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: That's a violinist, named Kurt Coble. He's a composer. His dream was always to write scores for horror films. He's now been at Phantom for 22 years, long enough to see three people in his section die.

segments.speaker: Kurt Coble
segments.text: When I'm playing the show, nobody's interested in my creative input. I've often compared it to working in a hospice. It's just-- we just keep the show alive as long as we can.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: So here they all are, in this weird social experiment, trapped together for decades, 27 musicians crammed into this tiny space. A trumpet player told me it's like playing in a submarine. I've been down there, and you can barely turn around without knocking into something.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: In the pit, you notice everything. The way your neighbor blows out a spit valve, the way someone brags about their kids, the smell of someone's perfume-- every little annoyance, every perceived slight, accumulates.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: One of my favorite stories, which would drive anyone who has ever played in a band crazy-- there's this bassoon player who has sat next to the same clarinet player since 1988. She's convinced he plays half a note flat on every note he's ever played. He denies this.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: The person I talked to the most in the pit was Melanie, the oboist. She's one of the rare people you meet who has no real filter.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: So I was complaining about something which I imagine was that it was really cold. It's always really cold. And then, someone else from the orchestra said-- [SIGHS] I'm just so tired of the sound of your voice.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: You know? And I'm tired of the sound of my voice, too, so I kind of sympathize with her. Then, there was a violinist who got mad at me because I said I use Roundup in my garden. She's like-- [HUFFS] And she wouldn't speak to me for, I don't know, weeks.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: During most of our talks, Melanie was making reeds. It's an extraordinarily meticulous process. There's all sorts of medieval-looking tools and tiny bits of wood everywhere.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: Oboists are the most optimistic people in the world. Because every time they make a reed, they think that it might work. They usually don't, but anyway.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: This part, I-- oh, no, I'm skipping the most important part. You need to pick your color of thread. And it just makes all the difference, and I never know what color to pick. But this is the only fun that I have, so.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: [BLOWING ON REED]

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: That god-awful noise.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Melanie studied at Juilliard. She dreamed of being the principal oboist in the Metropolitan Opera or the Philharmonic. But she kept bombing her auditions. Her nerves got the best of her every time she was up for a big seat.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: And then, life and bills intervened. Phantom, in that way, is a very good job, in a field where there aren't a lot of good jobs anymore. It put Melanie's kids through college, paid her mortgage, and provided security while the music industry collapsed around her.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: But at the end of 30 years sitting just inches away from your coworkers, you lose all sense of proportion. Your enemies turn into monsters. For Melanie, the monster in the pit was always a trumpet player named Francis Bonny. Everything he did drove Melanie nuts, from the black biking shorts he wore in the pit, to always eating his dinner in the locker room with his back turned to her.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: Francis was a miserable son of a bitch. And at a certain point, he started wearing-- like, he put this black shade on the side of his glasses. And he's wearing those things because he doesn't want to see me, right? That's why he's wear-- I really, truly believe this.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: I wanted to run this all by Francis. It just seems so unreasonable. Francis is the only person I had talked to who had actually escaped from the pit. He got in a truck and drove out to the middle of nowhere in Colorado. He says he's much happier now.

segments.speaker: Francis Bonny
segments.text: You spoke with Melanie! Oh!

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: (LAUGHING) Yeah, yeah, we did. I understand that you two did not have the best relationship. One of the things that she told us was that you basically made an eye patch, so that you wouldn't have to look at her. Is this a true story that she's telling us?

segments.speaker: Francis Bonny
segments.text: I did do that at some point. But that wasn't just because of Melanie. She's taking it too personally. It was actually anybody that was on my right.

segments.speaker: Francis Bonny
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: She told us, for a long time, that you sat in the locker room, and that you would turn your back to everybody, because you didn't want to look at them.

segments.speaker: Francis Bonny
segments.text: Yeah, yeah, it was in the locker room. I came there, I ate my dinner, looked at the white wall, went in, played the show, and then left the theater, left the premises as fast as I could. And it worked beautifully.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Can you compare the relationships that you have with other relationships?

segments.speaker: Francis Bonny
segments.text: It's family. [LAUGHS] It's your spouse you can't stand. And putting up with people that you just don't want to hear their voice again. You sit there. Thousands and thousands and thousands and thousands of hours. This is like a quarter of a lifetime.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: The musicians in the pit don't play the whole time, which means there are thousands of hours where they're not actually doing anything. And during those rests, they read books-- spy thrillers and mysteries-- and do the crossword with their neighbors.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: A trumpet player has taught himself three languages. Another musician ran a woodshop business on his laptop during the show. And socially, it's a bit like middle school. There are the loners, the jocks, and the French horns. They're like the boys in the back of the bus.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: They bring in fart machines and run the same practical jokes over and over. Sometimes they even mess with the audience. The front row is right up against the pit, so close that their feet sometimes dangle next to the musicians' heads. Occasionally, one of the French horn players would take out a bottle of Wite-Out and write little messages on the soles of the audience's shoes.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: Those guys-- they're sitting right behind me-- they're always chattering and laughing. I, being me, if I play badly, I think, oh, god, they're saying how terrible I am. Oh, god, I don't want to humiliate myself.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: This, more than anything, Melanie told me, is what makes her want to sound good every night. She's worried the French horn guys will make fun of her.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: I'm not playing for the audience, because the audience doesn't know. And so I'm playing for those French horn players. I do want to say, one of the compliments I've gotten over the years is, how do you still play so well when you've just been doing Phantom for all those years? I say, it's a choice that I've made. My choice is to play this music like it's any other music that I play, and make it beautiful.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Can you just play something from Phantom?

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: Well, I can play the really hard ones. If it's really bad, though, I beg you not to--

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: [PLAYING OBOE]

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: During the pandemic, like the rest of Broadway, Phantom shut down. The unstoppable show was put on pause for a year and a half. I checked in with Melanie during that break. She wasn't doing very well. She wasn't getting paid by the show.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: And she missed Phantom. This was surprising to me. Melanie and all the other musicians had told me about their fantasies of finally leaving the show, and I had believed them. But now that it actually happened, she missed the routine.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: You know, Phantom-- I miss the comradeship, the repetition of the silly jokes, and watching everyone eat. And I don't know. The routine-- I kind of like routine in my life.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: This, of course, is the opposite of what she'd said in the past, before COVID.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: It was always easy to complain that it was boring and to complain about driving into the city and wasting all that time in the car, and playing the same music, and going home again. And I just thought-- I knew I was lucky back then, but it becomes very real now. I mean, what can I say? Now, I really know what it's like not having this job.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: It's just so much fun to complain about things that don't matter. Oh, the women in the bathroom, they're just always talking about their expensive hair and makeup. And I miss the women in the bathroom. And yeah, I'd be happy to complain about that again.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Before the pandemic, every time I talked to Melanie, I would ask how she was doing. Her answer always depended on parking. It's hard to park in Midtown, Manhattan. A good parking spot was a good day. A bad parking spot was a bad day. This is how she made sense of her life.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: I think about this all the time. Most of our lives are spent finding parking for the job we don't want to do. Melanie's not alone in that. And after any number of years, those routines accumulate, and that's more or less your life.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Of all the people I talked to in the pit, one musician dealt with the mundane and inevitable repetition of life in a way that really stuck with me. For the past two decades in the pit, Kurt, the musician who described himself as a violin operator, has been dreaming up the most elaborate and metaphorically perfect coping mechanism. It's a band made up entirely of automatons. I met these robot musicians in a warehouse in Yonkers.

segments.speaker: Kurt Coble
segments.text: The PAM Band.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: The PAM Band stands for Partially Artificial Musicians. Kurt's automatons are made up of scraps of metal and string, all wired up to a soundboard that Kurt can program to create whatever sounds he wants. There's Magnus, an electric chord organ, Krieg, the bass guitar, and then there's Rosie, the theremin.

segments.speaker: Kurt Coble
segments.text: This is Jack, a solid-body electric violin using the exoskeleton design. This is what helps alleviate the boredom of the redundancy of Phantom. Because I'm constantly thinking about this project and how I can improve the automation and the kind of music that I would like to create.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Why did you decide to do this?

segments.speaker: Kurt Coble
segments.text: If I ever see a therapist, maybe they will help me understand that.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Let's pretend I'm a therapist.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Like, was there part of it where you're like, man, I am playing in this orchestra, I'm not-- it's not the expressiveness that I want, I also kind of feel like an automaton? You know? And maybe I just make an automaton as a violinist.

segments.speaker: Kurt Coble
segments.text: Sure, yeah. I mean, I can see exploring that-- am I looking for some kind of soul healing from this dehumanization of being in a violin section? Possibly. [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: I asked Kurt if the PAM Band could play "The Music of the Night," or "All I Ask of You," or any of the Phantom classics. He wasn't into that, at all. This band was not designed to play Andrew Lloyd Webber.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: But something inside him just couldn't get away from Phantom of the Opera. Back when he was sitting in the pit, he'd composed, just in his head, both the prequel and the sequel to Phantom, both which involve Indiana Jones-type characters.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: And years ago, he got a copy of the 1925 silent film version of Phantom and wrote an entire score. He wanted to play it for me. He turned off the lights in the warehouse and projected the film onto the wall. The PAM Band started to play.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: The score features him, Kurt, as a solo violinist and the star of the show. The automatons all play the same thing, but Kurt always improvises. None of his shows are ever the same.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Jay Caspian Kang is a staff writer for The New Yorker and co-host of the podcast, Time to Say Goodbye. His story was produced by Miki Meek.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So we first broadcast that story three years ago. And now, the decades of repetition in the Phantom of the Opera pit are finally coming to an end. After 35 years, the longest-running show in Broadway history is closing this week. Curious how the musicians in the pit were taking the news, Jay caught up with Melanie, the oboe player, when she just had four shows left to play. Jay asked about the moment when everybody who works on the show heard definitively, during a big Zoom meeting, actually, that the show was finally closing.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: What was your first thought? Because I remember that we had talked about it, and you sort of-- you and Lowell and Pete had all sort of fantasized about it. Because I asked you about this a lot, just like, well, what are you going to-- like, when you leave, how is it going to feel?

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: And so like, how did it actually feel? Like, 'cause you finally got confirmation that, OK, this is actually going to end.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: So the first thing is the dropping-of-your-gut-into-the-cellar kind of feeling, of shock, just complete shock. Like the-bottom-is-falling-out-of-my-world kind of feeling. I was upset.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: So what I do-- I said, I don't want to be sad, so I will be angry. Let's choose anger. And I said, I'm going to focus on all the things I hate. And that way, I won't be sad. And so that's what I did.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Well, did it work? Like, did it work to--

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: Yeah, I was so successful.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: --to just focus on everything you hate, instead of whatever feelings of sadness or regret or even fear that might have popped up?

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: No, this is at the beginning. OK, so, I was so good, right? I was so successful. Now that it's imminent, I do feel different. So now, it's much more of a rollercoaster up and down. Right now, there's all kinds of exciting activities going on.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: And then, you can sort of forget that it's closing. I am certainly sad about it. It's an entire way of life. I can't even really imagine knowing it will never be back. But most of those people, I'm never going to see again.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: Are people being nicer to one another in the pit?

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: Thank you for asking. [LAUGHS] People are being so nice. I'm trying to be quieter about things that annoy me, but fewer things are annoying me. And it's all very festive and fun.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: We had a really fun photo op on Friday. They had a full company photo call, so. I really enjoyed it, because everybody was up on stage. They all gave us a poster, and everyone's getting their posters signed like your high school yearbook.

segments.speaker: Jay Caspian Kang
segments.text: You know, when I first interviewed you several years ago, one of the things that you told me that made me laugh a lot was that you, after playing 20-something years at the time of the show, had never actually seen the show. And that sort of blew my mind, because I was like, how do you go every night? Like, you've never actually seen the show?

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: Yeah. So I realized that I really wanted to see the show, and I asked the management, and they set me up at the soundboard. And it was wonderful. This is just last week, I think.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: And what amazed me was the pageantry of it, the beauty of it. I had no idea. You see them bringing in all the ice backstage, outside of the stage door, every day. So there's a giant ice container, the dry ice, and then they carry it in.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: And then, we used to complain about the smoke. But I never knew what the smoke did. And so it creates this incredible atmosphere, and then there's all these lights. Like, we see the candelabra under the stage, but they're not lit under the stage.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: And so I got to see them on the stage. And I got to see the Phantom and Christine at the end of-- I don't know which number it was, but they just disappear. I mean, it's a trapdoor, but you have this effect that they're just disappearing. And I feel like a little kid, in a way-- just awestruck by all these things that other people have seen so many times.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: 11 people who are going to be in the pit closing night are musicians who were there on opening night, back in 1988. I was able to reach Lowell Hershey, who, as Jay pointed out in the story, everybody calls the sanest person in the pit. Like Melanie, Lowell has other gigs lined up for after Phantom closes, here and there. Nothing big, nothing too challenging.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Neither of them imagines playing for another Broadway show, either as a sub or as a regular player. Lowell, I have to say, was very chill about the closing.

segments.speaker: Lowell Hershey
segments.text: You know, I can't say that I didn't enjoy going to work. I did. It's fun for me to do that, and so I will miss that. But you know, I think I can find other things that will interest me. I don't feel like I'll be bored.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: How old were you on the first opening night?

segments.speaker: Lowell Hershey
segments.text: I was 40.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Can I ask you to go back and imagine, for a second, 40-year-old you on the opening night of Phantom? If you could somehow have said to him, you will be here for 35 years, and you'll be here on closing night of this show, what would that 40-year-old have said?

segments.speaker: Lowell Hershey
segments.text: Well, I would have been really happy to have heard that. Because at the time Phantom opened, I had an 11- and a 13-year-old-- two kids, and college was coming up. And if you told me that Phantom was going to go more than just a few years, and go 35, I would have been thrilled, because that would have meant that I would have some security. So yeah, I would have been very happy to have that information.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coming up-- a mom goes underground, goes undercover, to get an urgent message to her daughter. That's in a minute from Chicago Public Radio, when our program continues.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Today's program-- "What Lies Beneath," the stories of things and people, usually hidden from view, coming to the surface. We've arrived at Act Two of our program. Act Two, "How I Met My Mother."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So in some families, what's buried deep below are the true feelings that people have about one another. There's so many people out there who have trouble saying directly what they really feel. One of the producers here at our show, Elna Baker, comes from a long line of passive-aggressive communicators.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: By the way, they know this. They own it. When her grandmother wanted to get a message across, a message like, don't leave change lying around, one time, she put an article on the fridge saying, "Toddler Chokes on Penny," and then just left it to everybody else to connect the dots.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Elna's mother communicates in the same indirect way, which became a problem in the years after Elna left the church. Elna's family's Mormon, and her mom had some important things that she wanted to say to her. Here's Elna.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: This all started when I made a joke about me buying weed to my brother. Careful, he said. If Mom were to hear that, she'd send an email to the whole family about how you're an addict. I laughed. And then, I was like, wait, what? That was way too specific.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Did Mom send an email to the whole family about me being an addict? And he was like, uh, mm, nothing, never mind, which could only mean one thing. She did. It took several rounds of questioning before I got the whole story.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: The email he was referencing-- my mom had sent it 10 years ago. At the time, I was about to host a comedy show in New York, where me and a bunch of performers would play drinking games on stage. It was called The Drunk Show.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: The show was being promoted online. My mom, a devout Mormon, saw an article about it and freaked out. Mormons don't drink. It's against the religion.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And what I learned from my brother, years after the fact, is that my mom was so worried that I was doing this show, she sent an email to my family, my extended family, uncles, cousins, and family friends who I grew up with, like the Mitchells, the Coxes-- Heidi, my middle school drama teacher.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: "Dear friends," it begins. "I am writing, because I am concerned about the direction Elna's life has turned. She is spiraling downward, fast."

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: My mom then explains to them that I'm doing this event called, The Drunk Show, then writes, "I am very concerned. In our family, you are either an alcoholic or a Mormon. And I think she may be headed in the wrong direction. I don't know what I can do personally. She doesn't hear me."

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I'm going to interject here-- that I didn't hear her, because she never said anything to me about it. In the email, she inserts a link to the article about The Drunk Show, and then reveals her grand master plan. She's been commenting on the article, under fake names, warning me not to do the show.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: "Can everyone else please make up fake accounts and also comment? This way, I'll cancel the show." She ends, "Thanks. Pray for us both, please."

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: When I read this email, I was mortified. I drink socially. I'm not an alcoholic. But since I'd never intercepted the email, I worried everyone who got it had thought this for years. I immediately clicked on the link to the article.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: At the bottom of the page, there were four comments from four different people, trolling me, all clearly my mother. Her first fake character is Carol from the West Village, who says, quote, "Encouraging irresponsible drinking that could end in hospitalization of performers is an invitation to a lawsuit. Don't be idiots."

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: The three other comments escalate from there. Here's the weirdest part. She wrote all these comments while she was staying with me. She was in town the week of The Drunk Show. We slept in the same bed. But she didn't say a word to me about it.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: As interventions go, it was the least successful one I've ever heard of or could imagine. No one else among the family or friends chimed in. And I, the target of the intervention, never knew it happened. I never heard of or read the comments online until my brother accidentally let it slip, years later.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Since I found out about this, I've wondered why my mom chose to communicate this message to me the way she did. But I've never asked her, because I figured it would just lead to a fight and no answers. But we're much closer now than we were when I did The Drunk Show. Why not try?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: To my surprise, she agreed to talk about it, but on these conditions. Dad had to be there, in case we needed mediation. I had to come home for Christmas in exchange. And most importantly, I could only do this story if she got to write the ending, which we'll get to later.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Talk for a second?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Hi, Elna. How are you?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Wow, Mom, you got sexy.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Wow, Mom.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: I'm trying out a lower voice, because I think my voice is too screechy.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Don't do that. (LAUGHING) Don't spend the whole interview not being yourself.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We started at the beginning. How did my mother decide that anonymous comments online would be the best way to reach me? She said my sister, Julia, told her about The Drunk Show.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: So I'm laying there on the couch. I'm at your apartment, probably about 5:00 in the morning. And I'm stewing over this. I can't sleep. I haven't slept for hours.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: And then, I just had this little epiphany. I can put this on here in somebody else's voice. I don't have to use my own voice. And then, maybe she'll take it seriously. You just need to hear it from New Yorkers.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Oh, come on, Elna. You're from New York, you live in New York, and you value their opinions.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: More than yours?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Oh, absolutely. Because I'm this fuddy-duddy, old-fashioned Mormon lady that doesn't know anything. You know? I'm, like, from 1950. I'm like June Cleaver.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Are you saying that you are like that, or that I think-- you think I think that?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: That's what I think you think I am, yeah.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Before things get too tense, my mom and I pull up the comments page together.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: So now, let's look at these--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The first thing I learned was how fleshed out these people were in my mom's mind. Like, Carol from the West Village, who warned that irresponsible drinking could lead to lawsuits--

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: She's a lawyer. Because that's the way a lawyer would say things, isn't it?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: She's dealt with lawsuits that have involved drunk drivers or something with alcohol involved, right?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: To be clear, nowhere in the comments does it say Carol is a lawyer. For each entry, there's just a name and location, like Don from the Upper West Side.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Pretty ritzy area, right?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Mm. Who is Don in your mind?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Don is a comedian--

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Oh. OK.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: --who's older. He used to do, kind of, the old-style comedy.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Again, reading the comments, you'd never know Don was a comedian.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Yeah, he's just disgusted with how comedy has evolved in the last 15 years or so.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: What does Don think about me doing this show?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: He says, "Comedy, where you're laughing at the performers and not with the performers, is not comedy. It is tragedy. Is this really what NYC comedy is reduced to? Are you really not cleverer than this?"

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Why did you think, like, Don saying this to me would reach me?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Well, you love comedians. I mean, it's all about the comedy for you.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: So of course, if this is not going to be funny, then maybe we shouldn't do this.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: The next comment comes from the East Village, from a commenter named, Please.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: OK, so I'm thinking this is a policeman.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And his name is Please?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Yeah, Officer Please.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: It doesn't say, "Officer," Mom. (LAUGHING) It just says, "Please."

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: What-- why is this policeman writing me? Why is he so offended by this show?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Well, he says, "10 years after 9/11, and this is where New York is? Come on."

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: The show is on September 17.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: "I think this week, of all weeks, we should all be a little more sensitive and full of introspection."

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: OK. Um, can we just-- I think we can both agree that you went-- you went real big on this one.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: I hit the 9/11 button.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Her last comment is a straight-up Mormon talking point. Alcoholism and all other addictions take away freedom of choice. Seven minutes after she posted that, she sent the mass email. My mom said she went so hard because--

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: So I have two uncles who died of alcoholism poisoning. My uncle died at age 30. My other uncle came to my wedding completely drunk and ended up dead about two years later, from alcoholism. Gary's grandfather died of alcoholism.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: So that's how I get there. It's not like it's a Mormon thing. It's an experience that has affected me. It affected my mother. She was just devastated over her brother and his alcoholism.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Stopping The Drunk Show meant stopping me from becoming one of these people. My mom says she saw the promo photo of me sipping a drink on the page announcing the show, and thought--

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Has she lost her mind? She has relatives who died of alcoholism. She's been taught since she was little girl to be careful around alcohol. Has she completely blocked out everything I've ever taught her?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Did you ever consider just calling me?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Elna, we've already been there. You don't hear me! You just don't hear me. It's just a joke. You have to hear it from somebody who you think is credible.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Come on. Admit it, Elna. You know you would have just laughed. You would have called Kevin, you would have had a good laugh, and you would have had the show anyway.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: But you didn't-- the thing--

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Come on, admit it.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Wait.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: You know it. You know you would have rolled your eyes at me.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: But you didn't even try.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: But Elna, just-- just tell me. What's the truth on your end?

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Well, I don't think I-- here's the thing. I think if you just told me not to do it, I would have-- I would have done exactly what you're saying. But if we'd had a full conversation where we really talked-- like, so for example, I didn't know until just now, until we've had this conversation-- like, I didn't really know that much about your family history with drinking.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: You don't talk about these unpleasant things, so that when you're so against drinking, I think I did think it was just had to do with Mormonism, and not that it had to do with really painful things you witnessed in your life. Because you never told me about them.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: I'm sure I've said this statement before in your life. In our family, you're either a Mormon or an--

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Alcoholic.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Alcoholic.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Yeah, you heard that one before.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Yeah, I just didn't believe it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She'd said this to me all my life, but I was missing the context. I've never met any of these family members who drank. I don't remember her ever mentioning any of these stories. I saw my mother as sheltered. Almost all her friends are Mormon. I just thought she doesn't know what she's talking about, which was unfair.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When I make a radio story, I listen to my interviews over and over again. And this time, something unusual started to happen. With each listen, my mother sounded less and less like my mother.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Like, I stopped hearing her the way I usually do-- rolling my eyes, getting defensive. And I actually started to hear what she had to say. This is the line that struck me the hardest.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Elna, we've already been there. You don't hear me.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: She's right. And I can hear in her voice that this has been hurting her feelings for years. And that's my fault. I see why she thinks it's hopeless to talk to me about drinking, about anything. I'm incredibly dismissive. That's my part in this.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And her part-- she was totally upfront about that. She didn't want to confront me about drinking, because she has so much trouble with confrontation of any kind, with anyone, going back to when she was young.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: I mean, as a little kid, I used to just admit fault to anything that happened in our family in order to get the confrontation to be over with.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I never understood before this conversation what that feels like for her. She panics, feels trapped, like she needs to run, tightness in her chest, which is what makes this conversation so hard.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: This is-- we're doing exactly what I hate to do.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: What?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Talk about conflict. [CHUCKLES]

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: So what's happening to you when we do it?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Well, let's see, I'm twiddling my thumbs, right? I'm feeling my neck turn to stone.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: This cord, which is already coiled up, has been triple-coiled--

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: --for the headphones.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: [CHUCKLES] So yeah.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Well, thank you for putting yourself in your most uncomfortable place.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: Sure. You're welcome, Elna. Anything for my daughter.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: I knew what this meant. From the tone of her voice, it was time to stop. This was the most direct conversation I've ever had with my mother and the longest real conversation we've ever had. She'd gone above and beyond and did something she did not enjoy, for me. I could return the favor and call it a day.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Well, folks, my ticket home for Christmas is booked. And now, for the ending my mother requested-- it comes down to three words-- "She was right." Not about me spiraling downward fast, but about The Drunk Show.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: For the record, The Drunk Show was a disaster. I was the one who organized the drinking games, but because I'd only recently left the church, I was brand new to drinking. And all the penalties in the games were things like, take four shots of whiskey.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: Things went off the rails quickly. A performer threw a chair at an audience member. I drunk-dialed my ex from the stage, and the call went so badly, that I started crying in front of the audience. Ira, who was in the show, got blackout drunk-- for the first time in his life, he said-- and then threw up into a trash bag.

segments.speaker: Elna Baker
segments.text: And someone ended up in the hospital. My mom knew none of those details, of course. But big picture-- Carol from the West Village knew what she was talking about when she said irresponsible drinking can lead to hospitalization. In other words, Mom was right.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Elna Baker is one of the producers of our show and the author of the book, The New York Regional Mormon Singles Halloween Dance.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: ["JUST UNDER THE SURFACE" BY VENICE]

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, our program was produced today by Aviva DeKornfeld and Lina Misitzis. The people who put together today's rerun include Alaa Mostafa, Stowe Nelson, Matt Tierney, and Diane Wu. Our managing editor is Sarah Abdurrahman. Our senior editor is David Kestenbaum. Our executive editor is Emanuele Berry.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Our website-- thisamericanlife.org, where you can hear over 700 episodes of our program for absolutely free. This American Life is delivered to public radio stations by PRX, the Public Radio Exchange.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Thanks, as always, to our program's co-founder, Mr. Torey Malatia. He and I were talking the other day, and he let slip, he has not been listening to our program for weeks. Weeks! I was like, what? Totally confronted him about it. And I don't know. I guess he had a good reason.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: [SIGHS] I'm just so tired of the sound of your voice.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I'm Ira Glass. Back next week. I told Torey, I get it.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: You know, and I'm tired of the sound of my voice, too, so I kind of sympathize.

segments.speaker: Melanie Feld
segments.text: ["JUST UNDER THE SURFACE" BY VENICE]
